1:1: John assumes that Gaius will know who he is when he calls himself The elder. (See the Introduction to 3 John for a discussion of how to translate the term elder.)
Gaius is the name of a man, a fellow believer to whom John is writing this letter.
1:3: John is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith. In this case, these brothers were probably all male.
Here, walking on a path is a metaphor for how a person lives his life.
1:4: John speaks of those whom he taught to believe in Jesus as though they were his children. This also emphasizes his love and concern for them.
Here, walking on a path is a metaphor for how a person lives his life.
1:5: John is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.
1:6: Here, to send on is an idiom that means to provide people with what they need for a journey.
1:7: John is referring specifically to the name of Jesus. He is using the term name by association to mean Jesus himself.

John assumes that Gaius will know what he means by receiving nothing from the Gentiles. This could mean: (1) that the traveling believers had resolved not to accept any help from unbelievers; (2) that people who did not believe in Jesus would not help these traveling believers.
Here, Gentiles does not mean people who are not Jewish. It refers to any people who do not trust in Jesus.
1:8: John assumes that Gaius will know that when he tells him to support these believers, he means that Gaius should provide hospitality, including giving them what they need for their journey.
John is speaking as if the truth were a living thing that he and his fellow Christians could become workers with.
John is using the term truth to represent something or someone associated with the truth. This could mean: (1) the true message from God; (2) God himself, who is Truth.
1:9: What John wrote was a letter, probably containing instructions about helping traveling Christian teachers.
Here, the church refers to Gaius and the group of believers who regularly met together with him to worship God.
Diotrephes is the name of a man who was a leader of the church.
John is using the word first in the sense of “most important” or “in charge.”

John is using the word us to represent someone or something associated with himself and those with him. This could mean: (1) that Diotrephes opposes providing hospitality and support to the traveling believers whom John endorses. (The word translated receive in this verse is the same one as in the phrase “he does not receive the brothers” in the next verse.); (2) that Diotrephes does not accept John’s authority and so will not do what he says.
1:10: John is using the term words to mean what Diotrephes has been saying by using words. These words are an example of the works that he is doing.
John is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.
1:12: John says all here as a generalization for emphasis.
John is speaking of the truth as if it were a living thing that could testify that Demetrius is a good person.
1:13: John is using something associated with a letter, the ink and pen he would use to write a letter, to represent the letter itself.
1:15: John ends his letter with a blessing for Gaius.
John assumes that Gaius will understand that by The friends in this instance, he means the believers who are with him.
John assumes that Gaius will understand that when he says the friends in this instance, he is referring to the believers who are there with Gaius.
